authoredFrom: code and two runs: the claim shape was observed in a token issued by better-auth 1.6.26 and verified from a Cloudflare Worker (agentpod#331), and the control pair moved from reserved to issued when grants became data the issuer can read (principal_grants)
purpose: One issuer, and every other plane verifies offline against a JWKS (charter decisions/2026-08-15-one-issuer-and-offline-verification.md). The moment a second plane reads a claim, the claim's NAME is a contract: a rename in the hub is a silent authorization failure in kaambaan, which fails in the direction that looks like the caller having no permission. This corpus is what makes that a failing test instead.

howToRead.issued: Claims the issuer MUST put in every token, and consumers may rely on. A missing one is a malformed token. NOTE the difference between a claim that is ABSENT and one that is EMPTY: absent means this issuer does not speak the control pair, empty (`[]` / `false`) means this principal is permitted nothing. Reading the first as the second would let an old issuer silently authorise everything.
howToRead.standard: Registered JWT claims the issuer sets. Consumers MUST validate iss, aud and exp.
howToRead.reserved: Names that are SPOKEN FOR and not yet issued. A token must not use them to mean anything else, and a consumer must not infer permission from their absence.
howToRead.reject: Tokens a consumer MUST refuse. These are the point of the corpus — a fixture of only-valid examples proves almost nothing.

algorithm.source: observed in agentpod#331; better-auth's jwt plugin default
algorithm.note: Consumers MUST pin the algorithm rather than trusting the token header, or a token signed with `alg: none` — or with a key of the consumer's choosing — is accepted.

issued.meaning: The principal acting. Today this is the Better Auth user id in AgentPod's hub; when the Organization plane mints principals it becomes that id, and this corpus changes with it.

What kind of principal `sub` names. Present because this suite exists to make humans and agents both first-class — a consumer that cannot tell them apart cannot enforce separation of duties, which is what charter decisions/2026-08-14-approvals-cross-planes-as-events.md turns on.

AgentPod's local isolation boundary for this principal. NOT the organisation: the organisation is owned by the Organization plane and recorded on each product's tenant as an optional external mapping (agentpod migration 0036, kaambaan migration 0002).

First half of the control pair — which agents this principal may dispatch. Values are NAMESPACED by the plane whose id space they belong to: `agentpod:<stationKey>` is matched by AgentPod, `kaambaan:<agentId>` by kaambaan.

valueRules.namespaced: Every value carries a plane prefix. An UNPREFIXED value matches nothing anywhere — that was the retired CONTROL_PAIR_GRANTS format, and letting it keep working would mean a half-migrated deployment enforcing two different rules depending on which reader ran.
valueRules.unknownNamespaceIsIgnored: A consumer IGNORES a namespace it does not recognise; it must never deny on one. A plane that refused what it did not understand would break the day a third plane appeared, and a claim is read by more planes over time, not fewer.
valueRules.wildcard: One trailing `*` is a prefix wildcard that may not cross the `:` it was written inside: `agentpod:hermes:*` reaches every Hermes station and no OpenClaw one.
valueRules.emptyDenies: `[]` is a decision, and the decision is no. It is what an operator writes to suspend someone without deleting their grant.

issued.meaning: Second half of the control pair — whether this principal may grant an agent its reach. Both halves are required: dispatch control alone is decorative, because anyone who can grant an agent production credentials does not need permission to dispatch it.

standard.meaning: The issuer's base URL. Consumers MUST validate it.
Expiry. THE REVOCATION SLA: agentpod#331 proved a token issued before a session is revoked keeps verifying until it expires, because verification is offline by design.

reject.why: A token with `alg: none` carries no signature. Pin the algorithm; never take it from the header.
exp in the past. This is the whole revocation story — a consumer that ignores exp has no revocation at all.
A validly signed token from another issuer is still not ours.
A token minted for a different audience must not be replayable here.

Signed by a key not in the JWKS — including a key that WAS in it and has been retired. agentpod#331 found retirement propagates only as fast as each consumer's JWKS cache, so this case is reachable in normal operation, not only under attack.
A token that verifies but names no tenant is not a weaker caller, it is an unresolvable one. Refuse it rather than falling back to a default boundary.
`hermes:*` with no plane prefix. The retired format; it must match nothing rather than be read as this plane's.

A token from an issuer that predates the control pair. A consumer must not treat absence as an empty grant, nor as an unrestricted one — it means the issuer cannot answer, and the consumer decides its own posture.
